contributions.headingText: Adult granulosa cell tumour is a tumour composed of granulosa cells growing in a variety of patterns, admixed with a variable population of fibroblasts or theca cells.
8620/3 Adult granulosa cell tumour of ovary
2C73.Y & XH7DV5 Other specified malignant neoplasms of the ovary & Granulosa cell tumour, adult type

Tumours can occur at any age but are most common in perimenopausal women, who usually present with abdominal pain or estrogenic manifestations, typically uterine bleeding {21998762; 30500284}. Concurrent endometrial hyperplasia (seen in about one third of cases) or, rarely, endometrial endometrioid carcinoma can occur {25527364}. Androgenic manifestations (more common in cystic tumours) and haemoperitoneum due to rupture each occur in about 10% of patients {6548120; 30500284}. Patients may have elevated serum levels of β-inhibin {17306349}.
Adult granulosa cell tumour is the most common sex cord–stromal tumour and accounts for about 1% of all ovarian tumours.

Nearly all adult granulosa cell tumours harbour a recurrent somatic FOXL2 missense mutation (p.Cys134Trp) {19516027; 20693978; 26033501}; however, the mechanism of tumour formation remains unknown {14736745; 21763750}.

Most tumours are unilateral, with an average size of 10 cm. They are typically solid and cystic but may be solid or rarely entirely cystic. The solid areas are usually soft and tan to yellow. Haemorrhage is common {6548120}.

Tumours may show a variety of architectural patterns, which may be admixed. The most common pattern is diffuse, but cells may be arranged in cords or trabeculae, may form discrete islands (insular pattern), or may surround small spaces containing eosinophilic (or rarely basophilic) fluid or hyalinized material (Call–Exner bodies, microfollicular pattern). Less common patterns include gyriform and watered silk (undulating rows and cords), macrofollicular, sarcomatoid, and pseudopapillary {29132723}. A variable amount of fibromatous or thecomatous stroma is present {29708950}. Some adult granulosa cell tumours are predominantly spindled, closely mimicking a cellular fibroma {17717430}; others are predominantly cystic, typically lined by multilayered granulosa cells that may be associated with Call–Exner bodies or nests of tumour cells within the cyst wall {6548120}. Tumour cells usually have uniform, pale, round to oval nuclei with an irregular nuclear membrane and nuclear grooves, and scant cytoplasm. Mitotic activity is usually low. Some tumours have a striking nodular growth of cells with moderate to abundant pale cytoplasm that closely resembles thecoma {29708950}. Luteinized tumours show abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and often lack nuclear grooves {21804396; 7814191}. In these tumours, cords of granulosa cells are often seen at the periphery of the tumour, albeit frequently limited in number. Increased mitotic activity, bizarre nuclei, mucinous epithelium, and hepatic differentiation can occur {6309684; 10478669; 7680545; 15968196; 21623197}. A minor component resembling juvenile granulosa cell tumour may be seen. Reticulin stain highlights reticulin fibres around tumour nests, unlike in fibroma and thecoma (where there is staining around individual cells) {28700438}. High-grade transformation characterized by marked cytological atypia and high mitotic count has been described {31162286}.

Tumours are typically positive for FOXL2 {21378549}, calretinin, inhibin (although staining may vary in distribution and intensity), and SF1 {19033865; 23240671}. ER, pancytokeratin, CD99, and WT1 are frequently positive {8314261; 1384370; 22123727; 19033865}, and tumours can be positive for SMA, desmin, and CD10 {17885484; 7731938}. PAX8, CK7, and EMA are typically negative {12808064; 9656124}.
Demonstration of the characteristic FOXL2 point mutation may be helpful in selected cases {31846522}.

Essential: granulosa cells with typical nuclear features, growing in a variety of patterns.

Desirable: reticulin surrounding groups of cells; immunohistochemical positivity for sex cord markers.

This entity is staged according to the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification (see TNM staging of ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal carcinoma [[Brierley JD, Gospodarowicz MK, Wittekind C, editors. TNM classification of malignant tumours. 8th ed. Oxford (UK): Wiley-Blackwell; 2017.]]) and the FIGO staging system.

Most patients present with stage I disease, which is associated with a 10-year survival rate of about 90–95% and a recurrence rate of about 10–15%; the overall recurrence rate for all stages combined is 20–30%. Tumours have a propensity for late recurrence, typically > 5 years later, but in some cases after 20 years or more {26003143; 27297428}. Peritoneum, omentum, liver, and lung are common sites of extraovarian spread. Tumour stage is the most important prognostic factor, and tumour rupture in stage I tumours is particularly important. Tumour morphology, mitotic activity, and atypia are not independent prognostic factors of survival {22019525; 25347095; 27297428; 27729108}. For tumours with extraovarian spread, the presence of residual tumour after surgery appears to be significantly associated with recurrence {22019525}. Patients may be followed for recurrence by monitoring of serum β-inhibin levels {17306349}. High-grade transformation may be associated with aggressive behaviour {31162286}.
